text: Adam Knows Eve Has Done Wrong: Does Loving Someone Mean Having to Follow Her All the Way?
When Eve returns to Adam, she has fruit in her hand.
First she explains why she did not return at the appointed time.
The tree does not bring death as they have always been told.
The serpent ate its fruit and not only survived, but acquired human speech and the power to reason.
She herself has eaten it too, and feels that her eyes are brighter and her mind more open, as though she is moving toward a higher form of life.
Then she makes a request of Adam:
You should eat too.
Let us share the same fate and the same joy, just as we share the same love.
Otherwise, I have changed and you have not; the difference in our degree of being may separate us.
These words make the fruit a question about their relationship.
Whether to eat is no longer only a matter of how Adam responds to the prohibition.
It seems also to determine:
Whether the two of them still wish to belong to the same life.
Book 9 of *Paradise Lost* draws a clear distinction between Eve and Adam.
Eve is deceived.
The serpent reinterprets the prohibition, drawing on her desires for knowledge, freedom, status, and self-affirmation to make her believe that the fruit will bring advancement rather than death.
Adam does not undergo the same deception.
As soon as he hears Eve's account, he understands what has happened.
The garland falls from his hand.
His face turns pale.
He knows that she has broken the prohibition and judges that some enemy has deceived her.
Then, in his heart, he makes a decision:
I cannot be without you.
You are bone of my bones and flesh of my flesh.
Your condition cannot be separated from mine.
If death is joined to you, then death is as life to me.
This is not someone who does not know what he is doing.
He sees the wrong and its possible consequences.
What he truly cannot accept is remaining alive while Eve alone is lost.
This makes it difficult to call Adam's action simply weakness.
He does not eat to gain knowledge.
Nor because the fruit looks tempting.
What moves him is a real and profound relationship:
To lose Eve is, for him, almost to lose himself.
To explain this love entirely as infatuation would miss the force the poem deliberately preserves in it.
When someone we love has done wrong, been hurt, or begun to move toward destruction, turning away and saying:
This was your choice. It has nothing to do with me.
Doing so is not automatically nobler than entering the consequences together.
Love does, by its nature, bring another person's fate into one's own life.
It prevents us from calculating only:
How can I keep myself safe?
Adam moves us precisely because he is unwilling to leave Eve in her error while keeping himself intact.
Yet not abandoning someone and repeating her error oneself remain two different things.
A person can stay after a partner has done wrong.
Can stand beside her as she faces the consequences.
Can refuse to reduce her to her worst action.
Can take responsibility for their own part in the relationship and help her seek whatever repair may still be possible.
These are all ways of bearing something together.
They do not require:
To prove that we are still together, I must make the same error myself.
But Adam seems to see only two options:
Do not eat, and lose Eve.
Eat, and remain joined to her in the same fate.
If these two options exhausted every possibility, his decision would have a tragic grandeur.
The problem is that he does not first seek a third answer.
He does not turn to God.
Does not wait.
Does not ask whether, now that a wrong has been done, there might still be another way to bear it.
He first decides that the situation is beyond remedy, then brings his own action into that despair.
Milton makes this sequence very clear.
Adam first says:
I will surely die with you.
Only afterward does his thinking gradually grow calmer, and a succession of reasons begin to appear.
The serpent has eaten the fruit and still lives.
Perhaps the consequences of breaking the prohibition are not so grave.
Perhaps, because the serpent has already tasted it, the fruit no longer retains its original sacred character.
Perhaps God will not really destroy humankind, his most important creation.
Perhaps, if humankind is extinguished, the enemy will only mock the Creator.
These reasons are not devoid of logic.
But they all follow “I cannot be separated from you.”
Adam does not first weigh the evidence and then decide that the fruit might be safe.
He first decides to share Eve's fate, then builds a world in which that decision can seem less frightening.
This does not mean that every subsequent argument must be false.
But it reminds us:
Being able to give many reasons for an action does not mean that those reasons actually brought the action about.
Sometimes reasons are summoned only after a decision, to build it a road that appears to have been there from the beginning.
Hearing Adam's decision, Eve embraces him in tears.
She calls it a great test of love.
Adam's willingness to bear God's anger and death for her proves that they are one in heart and soul.
So she says:
Let us bear the same sin together, if it is indeed a sin.
These words make wrongdoing a means of proving love.
If Adam eats too, their unity will be confirmed.
If he refuses, he may seem to place his own safety before their relationship.
When a relationship can be proved only by repeating the other's error, refusing the error comes to be reinterpreted as refusing the person.
This exerts a powerful pressure.
It need not come through an explicit threat.
Eve even says that, if she truly believed the fruit would cause death, she would rather die alone than urge Adam to share it.
She is still deceived and believes she is inviting him to share a higher life.
So she cannot be portrayed as someone who knowingly uses love to make Adam do something harmful.
But her ignorance does not change the structure of the invitation:
The same action is treated as the same love.
“We are one” can express a relationship's deepest commitment.
The two no longer regard each other as objects that can be replaced at any time.
What happens to one will truly change the other.
But if “oneness” is understood to mean that they can only make the same decisions, the relationship begins to cancel the two people who constitute it.
Adam says:
To lose you is to lose myself.
The words are moving.
But they also give Eve's condition the power to prescribe Adam's.
She has eaten, so he must eat too.
She may die, so he too must choose death.
Otherwise, they will no longer be one.
Yet is it not precisely because there are still two people here, able to answer, to dissuade, and to disagree at a crucial moment, that they can love each other?
If every difference is treated as a rupture in the relationship, intimacy will finally amount to nothing more than moving in step.
A truly shared fate need not require shared wrongdoing.
It can also mean:
Your error will enter my life. I will not pretend that I am wholly unaffected.
I will bear with you the reality it has created.
But I will not surrender the judgment I still possess to that error just to make us look the same.
This is not judging the other person from above.
On the contrary, it may preserve an ability that matters to both:
When one person has already been carried away by a particular judgment, there is still another position within the relationship from which to say:
Wait.
We do not have to commit the one error still unmade in order to prove our loyalty to each other.
If two people can only remain in agreement on every action, a mistake by either will automatically become their shared direction.
Such a relationship may look inseparable.
But it has also lost the possibility of mutual correction.
After Adam eats the fruit, earth and sky respond with ominous signs.
Milton again states explicitly:
He acts against his better knowledge, not deceived, but overcome by his feelings for Eve.
The poem is not neutral about his decision.
It holds that love cannot justify disobedience.
But even if we do not fully accept the poem's theological judgment, what follows still matters.
Adam and Eve have eaten the same fruit and attained the “same condition” they sought.
Yet this agreement does not bring a deeper shared life.
What comes first is self-inflation, desire, and a new way of looking at each other's bodies.
Then comes shame.
They cover their bodies with leaves and begin to lose the ability to face each other at ease.
Finally, they quarrel.
Adam blames Eve for insisting on going off alone.
Eve asks why, if he was the one with better judgment, he did not firmly prevent her.
Adam then says:
I could have kept immortal happiness for myself, but chose death out of love for you. Now you blame me instead.
Sinning together has not made responsibility naturally shared.
Instead, it has given each of them new reasons to shift responsibility to the other.
This reveals another problem in Adam's choice.
When someone gives up their own judgment for a relationship, they can easily turn that surrender into a debt the other person owes them afterward.
I knew all along.
I did it because of you.
To avoid leaving you, I sacrificed being right.
And so an active choice, described at the time as made out of love, later becomes:
You must take responsibility for my choice.
Eve has indeed influenced Adam.
She has indeed invited him to eat with her.
But the poem explicitly says he was not deceived.
He knows, and chooses.
If he rewrites all of this as “you brought this on me,” then, after doing wrong, he once again makes Eve bear responsibility for where his decision came from.
Love cannot be proved by giving up one's judgment.
Nor is disowning one's own decision a way to repair things afterward.
Eve's reply has problems of its own.
She says:
Why did you not command me absolutely to stay?
If you foresaw the danger, you should have stopped me more firmly.
This hands responsibility for her earlier choice to seek independent action back to Adam.
When she set out, she insisted that she should not remain forever untested and did not wish to be treated as someone incapable of judging for herself.
After failing, she turns “you let me go” into Adam's fault.
Adam approaches the same result from the other side:
He first says that force has no place in free will, then immediately answers with a general judgment that women cannot handle freedom.
Both begin to use the other's choices to diminish their own responsibility.
At the end of Book 9, the poem says that they spend fruitless hours accusing each other, neither condemning themselves first, with no end to their argument in sight.
Within the same book, the poem turns the language of “we are one” into “it is all because of you.”
So this story cannot end with the simple injunction “do not lose your reason for love.”
Adam is not facing an ordinary temptation.
He believes that Eve is already moving toward death, and that a life without her is no longer one he wishes to continue.
Demanding that he readily stay behind and let Eve bear the consequences alone might also mean abandoning the relationship.
The real question is not whether love should influence judgment.
If love did not influence judgment at all, it would not be love.
The question is:
How should love enter judgment without gaining the power to make another person's judgment for them?
Adam may change his life because of Eve's fate.
But he need not necessarily make the error she has already committed his way of proving loyalty.
Equally, refusing to do wrong together must not become a form of moral superiority.
A person cannot stand in a place of safety and say:
I knew you were wrong all along. Everything that follows is your problem.
Preserving one's judgment only to preserve one's purity, while leaving all the consequences to the person who has already fallen, is not bearing something together either.
The truly difficult path may be:
Not to repeat the error.
And not to leave the person who made it.
To acknowledge that the two have separate responsibilities.
And also acknowledge that the error has entered their shared life.
This path is harder than “we will do it together.”
And harder than “you are responsible for yourself.”
For it allows neither agreement as an escape from judgment nor difference as an escape from the relationship.
Within the theological world of *Paradise Lost*, Adam could have refrained from eating and brought what had happened before God.
Later, the poem will also open a path through repentance, judgment, and redemption.
But the Adam of Book 9 does not know how these things will unfold.
He sees only that Eve has fallen and imagines the loss already beyond remedy.
“The situation is already irretrievable” stops him from looking for other actions.
This is one of despair's greatest powers.
It does not necessarily make a person do nothing.
Sometimes it makes a person actively complete a loss that has not yet occurred, because then, at least, they need no longer face difference and the unknown.
If the ending is decided anyway, better to choose the same fate oneself than wait for separation.
Through action, Adam turns uncertainty into certainty.
He also closes the last remaining place from which a different answer could be given.
Eve hopes to share the same fate.
Adam, too, wishes to remain with her.
Both wishes come from their relationship, rather than indifference to each other.
But a shared fate cannot mean only:
The same error must happen to both people.
A deeper togetherness may require precisely that the two can still differ at a crucial moment.
One says:
I have already come this far.
The other answers:
I will not abandon you, but neither will I let this path become the only one we can share.
Such an answer does not guarantee that the relationship can survive.
Nor that the wrong can be repaired.
It simply refuses to prove love by copying an error.
When Adam eats the fruit, Eve believes that her love has at last received its highest proof.
By the end of the book, they are arguing over who should bear responsibility for everything.
This change is no accidental irony.
When a relationship treats shared wrongdoing as proof of togetherness, once the wrong is done, both will discover:
They remain two people, each bearing fear, shame, and responsibility separately.
The agreement forced into being by their actions cannot bear their differences for them.
Love can make a person say:
Your fate will change mine too.
But it cannot therefore leave the two with only one source of action.
Truly refusing to abandon someone sometimes means precisely:
At the moment when error has already defined her, not allowing it to go on defining both of them.

*Textual basis: Book 9 of the twelve-book 1674 edition of John Milton's Paradise Lost. Particular attention is given to Eve's account on returning of how the serpent persuaded her, and her invitation to Adam to eat with her so that they may have “the same fate, the same joy, and the same love” (approximately 9.851–885); Adam's immediate recognition that she has been deceived, his initial decision to die with her, the arguments he subsequently develops about the fruit's consequences, and his explanation of his choice through their “oneness” (approximately 9.888–959); Eve's description of sharing “one sin, one error” as the highest proof of love, followed by Adam's eating with her “against his better knowledge, not deceived” (approximately 9.960–1000); and their subsequent experience of desire and shame, ending with mutual accusations and neither blaming themselves first (approximately 9.1001–1189). This essay examines the structure of action in Milton's own literary epic. It does not equate that epic with Genesis or present it as the sole interpretation of all Christian traditions.*
